carb-cycling.summary: Alternating high- and low-carb days around training to keep lifting hard while dieting, aiming for a leaner, fuller physique with muscle kept.

quick.overview:
Carb cycling means alternating higher-carbohydrate days, usually on hard training days, with lower-carbohydrate days. The appearance payoff people want is fat loss while holding on to muscle, giving a leaner, fuller-looking physique.

The chain runs through fuel and weekly calories: high days feed heavy training and refill glycogen (stored with water), low days pull weekly intake down and shift fuel use toward fat. It emerged in bodybuilding and spread to the wider fitness audience in the 2010s and 2020s. Reference summaries note that research on carb cycling itself is limited, and that the claimed benefits are mostly drawn from studies of related low- and high-carbohydrate diets. Day-to-day scale swings are largely attributed to glycogen-bound water.
quick.how: People place the higher-carb days on their toughest training sessions and the lower-carb days on rest or lighter days, keeping protein steady throughout. It is typically run alongside a lifting program as part of a cut, and most users track body weight and photos over several weeks to judge progress.
quick.risks: Described as generally safe short term for healthy people, though long-term effects are less studied. Sources advise professional guidance for people with diabetes, eating disorders or metabolic conditions. Rigid day-by-day food rules can be hard to sustain for some people.

angle.text: Physique athletes and lifters use carb cycling to fuel hard training while dieting, aiming for fat loss with muscle kept and a leaner, fuller look. High-carb days feed training and refill glycogen while low days lower weekly calories. Direct trials comparing it with steady dieting are limited.

refeed-days-diet-breaks.summary: Planned higher-calorie days or weeks during a cut, used to refill glycogen, keep dieting sustainable and look fuller while getting lean.

quick.overview:
Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of higher food intake, often extra carbohydrate, inserted into a calorie-restricted diet. People cutting for a lean look use them to look fuller, train better and stick with the diet long enough to finish the fat loss.

The chain: more carbohydrate refills glycogen, which is stored with water, so muscles look fuller and scale weight can rise short term. Proponents also say the break eases hunger and makes the diet easier to keep up, which sustains fat loss. A refeed usually lasts a day or two; a diet break is longer, such as a week at maintenance intake. The wiki's reference material is limited and no clinical study on appearance outcomes was located.
quick.how: Dieters schedule a refeed every so often, or a longer break after weeks of dieting, raising calories mainly through carbohydrate while keeping protein normal. Many pair it with hard training days and expect the fuller look within a day or so.
quick.risks: The documented drawbacks are practical: a refeed can stall the calorie deficit or trigger overeating. Scale weight rises temporarily from glycogen and water. People with eating disorders are generally advised against rigid diet cycles.

angle.text: Dieters schedule refeeds or diet breaks during a cut to look fuller and keep fat loss going. Extra carbohydrate refills glycogen and water in the muscles and makes the diet easier to stick with. They are common in bodybuilding and appearance-focused circles.

sodium-potassium-manipulation-peak-week.summary: Bodybuilder-style salt, potassium and water adjustments in the last days before a show or shoot to look drier and more defined, with real dehydration risks.

quick.overview:
Peak week is the final stretch of bodybuilding contest preparation, in which competitors adjust sodium, potassium, carbohydrate and water intake to look drier and more defined on stage. Some appearance-focused people borrow the idea for photo shoots.

The chain: changing electrolytes and fluids is said to shift how much water sits under the skin and in muscle, while carbohydrate loading in the final stage refills glycogen, which holds water, to make muscles look full. Reference sources describe the general approach only briefly, and no controlled study of the sodium and potassium part was found.
quick.how: It is done in the last days before the event, as the final phase of a long cut, with carbohydrate, salt and fluid intake changed on a planned schedule. People use it for a specific date, not as an everyday routine, and the visible change is expected on the day itself.
quick.risks: Intentional dehydration is among the practices linked in reference material to higher death rates among bodybuilders. Dehydration of even a few percent of body water can impair thinking and cause dizziness, and larger losses are dangerous. Electrolyte shifts carry their own health risks.

angle.text: Bodybuilders adjust sodium, potassium and fluids in the final days before a show or shoot to look drier and more defined, by shifting water under the skin. It is a documented part of contest prep, and practitioners report the visual effect; controlled studies of it are limited.

water-cutting-dehydration-pre-photo.summary: Limiting fluids shortly before a photo or show to look drier and sharper on camera; dehydration carries well-documented health risks.

quick.overview:
Water cutting means deliberately limiting fluids, sometimes alongside other measures, shortly before a photo, show or weigh-in so the body looks drier and more defined. It comes from physique sport and is sometimes discussed in appearance communities.

The chain: less water under the skin and in tissues is said to give a tighter, sharper look on camera. Body water loss does reduce blood volume and tissue hydration. It is described as the last stage of bodybuilding prep, and practitioners report the visual effect; no studies of its effect on appearance were found.
quick.how: People restrict fluids for the hours or days before the event, usually after a long cut and often alongside carbohydrate and sodium changes. It is used for a single occasion, with fluids returning to normal afterwards.
quick.risks: Medical sources report that losing 1 to 2 percent of body water can impair thinking, 5 to 8 percent can cause fatigue and dizziness, and losses above 10 percent can cause serious decline. Reference material links intentional dehydration to higher death rates among bodybuilders.

angle.text: Competitors and photo-minded users restrict fluids shortly before a shoot or contest to look drier and more defined on camera, by lowering water under the skin. It is the last stage of bodybuilding prep, and the visual benefit is reported by practitioners; dehydration has well-documented health risks.

whole-food-unprocessed-diet.summary: Eating minimally processed foods and cutting ultra-processed ones to get leaner, less bloated in the face and clearer-skinned.

quick.overview:
A whole-food or unprocessed diet builds meals from foods close to their natural form and avoids ultra-processed products. People adopt it for a leaner body, less facial puffiness and clearer, healthier-looking skin.

The chain runs through diet quality: cutting ultra-processed foods tends to lower calorie intake and improve what you eat overall, which supports leanness, and users report less bloating and better skin. Observational studies link high ultra-processed food intake with obesity and several diseases, though the category is debated, and no study has tested the appearance outcomes of cutting it.
quick.how: People shop around whole ingredients such as meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit, legumes and grains, and cook at home instead of buying packaged products. The NOVA classification, which groups foods by degree of industrial processing, is often used as a guide. Changes in leanness show over weeks to months.
quick.risks: No notable harms are documented for eating whole foods. Critics of the ultra-processed food concept note that some processed foods are nutritious and that broad condemnation can be oversimplified.

angle.text: Users switch to minimally processed foods for a leaner body, less facial bloating and better-looking skin. Cutting ultra-processed foods improves diet quality and lowers calorie intake, which is the route to leanness. Observational studies link ultra-processed food to weight gain; skin and face outcomes have not been tested.

clean-eating.summary: A whole-foods eating style, the chicken, rice and broccoli staple, that forums link to clearer skin and a leaner look.

quick.overview:
Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets built around whole, minimally processed foods, avoiding refined sugar, additives and convenience products. It began in 1990s bodybuilding as high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals such as chicken, rice and vegetables, and later spread through wellness books and social media. In looksmaxxing communities it is a baseline for leanness, skin and hormones.

The chain: whole foods and less added sugar mean better diet quality and fewer calories, which supports a leaner body, and forum users link it to steadier insulin, steadier hormones and fewer acne flares. These mechanisms are discussed in the community and have not been tested as a package. Published research mostly looks at how people define clean eating and how it relates to body image and eating behaviour.
quick.how: People eat simple ingredient lists built around lean meat, rice, vegetables and fruit, cook most meals themselves and cut added sugar, sometimes with extra exclusions such as gluten or dairy. Leaner body composition shows over weeks to months, with skin changes reported over a similar span.
quick.risks: Surveys and qualitative studies have linked rigid clean-eating beliefs with restrained eating and with orthorexia nervosa, a proposed (not formally recognised) eating disorder. Versions that cut out whole food groups have been criticised by commentators for possible nutrient gaps. Analyses of clean-eating blog recipes found nutrient profiles broadly similar to other recipes.

angle.text: Clean eating, the chicken, rice and broccoli staple, is used for a leaner body and clearer skin. Whole foods and less sugar improve diet quality and cut calories, and forum users link this to fewer breakouts. Research on its health effects is limited, and links to disordered eating have been flagged.

eat-the-rainbow-skin-nutrient-diet.summary: Eating many colours of fruit and vegetables for carotenoids and antioxidants, in hope of healthier-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Eat the rainbow means eating fruit and vegetables of varied colours, which carry different pigments and antioxidants, with the aim of better-looking skin and general health.

The chain: fruit and vegetables are good sources of vitamins C and E and carotenoids, and the idea is that these antioxidants and pigments counter oxidative stress in the skin. Carotenoid intake has been linked to skin colour. Trials of antioxidant supplements found no effect, or a small increase in mortality in vulnerable groups, and no skin studies of the colour-variety approach were found.
quick.how: People aim to get several colours on the plate each day, such as leafy greens, orange and red vegetables, berries and citrus, mostly as part of ordinary meals. Skin changes are reported after weeks of consistent intake.
quick.risks: Whole produce is generally not the concern; high-dose supplements are. The CARET trial found higher lung cancer rates in smokers taking beta-carotene and vitamin A. Cooking can destroy some vitamins while raising the availability of some carotenoids.

angle.text: Users eat varied colourful produce for its vitamins, carotenoids and antioxidants, hoping for healthier-looking skin. Carotenoid intake has been linked to skin colour, while antioxidant supplement trials showed no benefit; the colour approach itself has not been studied for skin.

oatmeal-fibre-for-gut-skin-axis.summary: Eating oats and other fibre to feed gut bacteria, in hope of clearer skin through a proposed gut-skin link.

quick.overview:
Fibre-rich foods such as oatmeal are eaten to feed gut bacteria, with the hope of clearer skin through a proposed gut-skin axis. It is a common talking point in appearance communities.

The chain: gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate), which are linked to gut-barrier and immune functions, and the idea is that this calms inflammation that could show up in the skin. Fibre has documented effects, including lower cardiovascular risk associations and relief of constipation, and oat beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol. Skin outcomes have not been studied in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: People add oats, barley, beans, vegetables and other high-fibre foods to daily meals, most often with oatmeal as breakfast. The change is gradual, and users report digestion effects first.
quick.risks: Inulin can cause flatulence and digestive distress above about 15 g per day, and isolated fermentable fibres may cause bloating and gas. Raising fibre gradually is the usual way people avoid this.

angle.text: Users eat oats and other fibre to feed gut bacteria that make short-chain fatty acids, hoping for clearer skin through a proposed gut-skin axis. Fibre has documented gut and cholesterol effects; its effect on skin has not been studied.

probiotics-fermented-food-for-skin.summary: Probiotic supplements and fermented foods such as kefir and kimchi, used for clearer skin and fewer breakouts through the gut.

quick.overview:
Probiotics are live microorganisms that confer a health benefit when given in adequate amounts, in the WHO's 2001 wording. Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, kimchi and sauerkraut contain live cultures. People use both foods and supplements hoping for fewer breakouts and calmer, clearer skin.

The chain: probiotics shift gut microbes, which is proposed to lower systemic inflammation and improve skin through a gut-skin axis. Research on probiotics and synbiotics for acne is described as preliminary, with possible reductions in inflammatory lesions and improved barrier function. For eczema, the American Academy of Dermatology does not recommend probiotics for established atopic dermatitis. Benefits are strain-specific.
quick.how: People eat fermented foods daily or take a probiotic capsule, often alongside fibre-rich foods and a general acne routine. Any skin change is reported after weeks of regular use.
quick.risks: Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in critically ill or immunocompromised people. Bloating and gas are common side effects at higher amounts. EFSA has rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.

angle.text: People take probiotics or eat kefir and kimchi hoping to calm inflammation and clear acne through a proposed gut-skin link. Gut microbes are thought to influence inflammation that reaches the skin. Acne research is described as preliminary, with some evidence in eczema.

gut-health-protocols-gut-skin-axis.summary: Bundled routines of food elimination, probiotics, fermented foods and fibre aimed at clearer skin through the gut.

quick.overview:
Gut health protocols combine steps such as removing suspected trigger foods, adding probiotics or fermented foods and eating more fibre, with the aim of clearer skin through the gut. They are discussed in skin communities under the label gut-skin axis.

The chain: gut bacteria and their metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, are proposed to affect immune and inflammatory signalling that could reach the skin. Gut-brain axis research relies heavily on animal models and small human studies, and its associations are considered correlational rather than causal. Elimination diets are an established diagnostic tool for food allergy, and probiotics for acne are described as preliminary research. No trials of the bundled protocols for skin appearance were found.
quick.how: People usually run it as a multi-step routine: cut suspected trigger foods for a period, add fermented foods or a probiotic, raise fibre intake, then reintroduce foods one at a time to see what the skin does. Users report judging results over several weeks.
quick.risks: Elimination diets need to stay nutritionally complete, and strict forms are generally not recommended in pregnancy. Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in immunocompromised people.

angle.text: Users bundle food elimination, probiotics, fermented foods and fibre to clear skin through the gut. The idea is that healthier gut microbes calm the immune and inflammatory signalling that reaches the skin. The gut-skin links are mostly associations.

elimination-diet.summary: Temporarily removing suspected trigger foods, then reintroducing them one at a time to find what sets off acne or flare-ups.

quick.overview:
An elimination diet removes suspected foods for a period, roughly two weeks to two months in Wikipedia's description, while symptoms are tracked, then reintroduces them one at a time to see whether symptoms return. In looksmaxxing communities it is used to find foods that worsen acne or other skin flare-ups, so people can cut their personal triggers and get calmer, clearer skin.

The chain: identifying a specific trigger food lets you remove it, which cuts the reactions that show up on the skin. The method is established for diagnosing food allergy and intolerance, and its best-documented clinical role is in gut conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis. Studies of finding skin triggers this way were not located.
quick.how: People cut a defined list of foods, keep a food and symptom diary, then challenge foods back in one at a time over weeks. It is often done with dietitian guidance, especially for stricter versions.
quick.risks: The diet must stay nutritionally complete, symptoms may briefly worsen at the start, and strict versions are generally not recommended in pregnancy. People with asthma, laryngeal oedema or a history of anaphylaxis may need testing where resuscitation is available. Unvalidated tests such as Vega machine testing have not been shown to be effective.

angle.text: Appearance communities use elimination diets to hunt for foods that set off acne or flare-ups, then reintroduce them one at a time to confirm. Finding and dropping a personal trigger is the route to calmer, clearer skin. The method is established for diagnosing food allergy; trials on skin triggers are limited.

low-histamine-diet.summary: An elimination diet that cuts aged, fermented and stored foods to reduce flushing, redness and skin symptoms people attribute to histamine.

quick.overview:
The low-histamine diet limits foods that are high in histamine or thought to trigger its release, such as aged cheese, fermented foods, cured meats and alcohol. People use it to reduce facial flushing, redness, itching and eczema-type skin symptoms, aiming for calmer, less red skin.

The chain: the proposal is that the enzyme diamine oxidase (DAO) fails to break down dietary histamine in some people, so histamine builds up and produces flushing and itching. Cutting high-histamine foods is meant to lower that load. This link has not been established, and no validated test exists. Studies are small and mostly uncontrolled, and histamine intolerance is not a formally recognised diagnosis.
quick.how: Followers eat fresh food, avoid stored leftovers and limit fermented foods, aged cheese, cured meats and alcohol, often for a trial period while noting symptoms. Published food lists differ from one another.
quick.risks: The main documented concern is restriction itself: food lists differ between sources and some excluded foods may not be high in histamine. Symptoms can overlap with allergies, mast cell disorders and gut disease, which clinicians evaluate separately.

angle.text: Users follow it to reduce facial flushing, redness and eczema-type skin symptoms they attribute to histamine, favouring fresh food and limiting aged, fermented and cured items. The aim is calmer, less red skin. The histamine-intolerance concept and its skin benefits are thinly studied.

paleo-diet.summary: A whole-food, no-grain, no-dairy diet of meat, vegetables, fruit and nuts, used for a leaner physique and less inflammation.

quick.overview:
The paleo diet builds meals from meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts and avoids grains, dairy, legumes and processed foods. It is popular in fitness and appearance communities as a whole-food route to leanness and clearer skin.

The chain: cutting processed food and several food groups lowers calorie intake, which researchers note is the main explanation for weight loss on the diet, and leads to a leaner body composition. Short trials report some metabolic changes. Wikipedia describes the research quality as poor to moderate, trials are small and short, and some anthropologists dispute the premise that it reflects how ancestral humans ate.
quick.how: People eat meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts, cook most meals themselves and skip bread, pasta, dairy and packaged foods. It is typically followed as a long-term eating style, with changes in body composition showing over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include lower calcium and vitamin D intake, side effects such as headaches and diarrhoea in one trial, and the cardiovascular associations of high red meat intake.

angle.text: Followers adopt paleo eating for a leaner physique and less inflammation, built on meat, vegetables, fruit and nuts. Cutting processed foods, grains and dairy lowers calorie intake, which is the route to leaner body composition. Short trials report some metabolic changes.

whole30.summary: A 30-day reset cutting sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and legumes, then reintroducing them, used for leanness, energy and clearer skin.

quick.overview:
Whole30 asks participants to eat only whole foods for 30 days, cutting added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and legumes, then to reintroduce them one by one. Its founders frame it as a reset for energy, digestion and cravings. In appearance circles it is used as a short clean-eating protocol for a leaner body and clearer skin.

The chain: removing processed foods and common trigger foods lowers cravings and calorie intake, which people report as a leaner look, and reintroduction is meant to show which foods affect them individually. It was created in 2009 by Melissa Hartwig (now Melissa Urban) and Dallas Hartwig. Wikipedia notes no studies had examined its health effects as of 2019.
quick.how: People follow the strict food list for the full 30 days, plan and cook meals in advance, then bring foods back in one at a time while noting how they feel. The founders discourage weighing and calorie counting during the month.
quick.risks: Dietitians have criticised its restrictiveness and the exclusion of whole grains and legumes. Independent studies on its physical risks are limited.

angle.text: People use Whole30 as a one-month reset, aiming for a leaner body, better energy and clearer skin, then reintroduce foods to spot personal triggers. Cutting processed foods lowers cravings and calories. Gains are mostly reported by users; the program has no controlled trials of its own.

bryan-johnson-blueprint-diet.summary: The mostly vegan, early-eating meal plan of longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, followed for biomarkers and a younger-looking, healthier appearance.

quick.overview:
The Blueprint diet is the largely vegan meal plan that Bryan Johnson follows as part of Blueprint, his longevity protocol. He publishes his meals, supplements and biomarker results. Looksmaxxers follow it as part of a routine aimed at slowing biological aging and keeping a youthful look.

The chain: Johnson says the aim is to lower the biological age of his organs through diet, exercise, sleep and supplements, and a lean, healthy body is the visible result people point to. Grokipedia describes three meals ending by 11 a.m. The results come from one person, and experts quoted in coverage say his biomarker changes do not establish slowed aging. No clinical trial has tested the diet.
quick.how: Followers copy the published structure: mostly plant-based meals, eaten early in the day, with the final meal finished by late morning, usually combined with Johnson's wider routine of exercise and sleep habits.
quick.risks: Coverage reports expert skepticism and some controversy around Blueprint products. The plan is restrictive in timing and food choice, and no trial data on the diet exist.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers follow Bryan Johnson's published mostly vegan, early-eating meal plan as part of a longevity routine aimed at slowing biological aging and keeping a youthful look. The evidence is his own tracked biomarkers; the diet has not been trialled in other people.

longevity-blue-zones-diets.summary: Plant-leaning eating patterns modelled on regions reported for long-lived residents, used to stay lean and look younger for longer.

quick.overview:
Blue Zones diets copy the largely plant-based eating of regions reported to have unusually many long-lived people, such as Sardinia, Okinawa and Nicoya. In appearance and longevity discussions they are used to stay lean and keep youthful-looking skin for longer.

The chain: plant-heavy food, physical activity, low stress and social ties are said to together support lower body fat and healthier aging, which shows in appearance. The idea originated in a 1999 Sardinia study, and Dan Buettner popularised it from 2005. Critics have questioned the accuracy of the age data, and reviews report no controlled trials of the diets; the diet's separate contribution has not been tested.
quick.how: People build meals around beans, vegetables, whole grains, nuts and olive oil, eat meat sparingly, and often borrow the lifestyle habits such as daily walking and shared meals. It is followed as a long-term eating style.
quick.risks: No specific harms are documented. Critics focus on the weak evidence and the commercial packaging of the concept.

angle.text: Users copy the plant-leaning eating patterns of long-lived regions in the hope of staying lean and looking younger for longer. The link to youthful skin and appearance is drawn from population observation, and the age data behind it have been questioned.

orange-juice-vitamin-c-diet.summary: Heavy orange juice or vitamin C intake to support collagen and brighten skin, based on vitamin C's role in collagen synthesis.

quick.overview:
This practice means taking in large amounts of orange juice or vitamin C to firm and brighten the skin.

The chain: vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that build collagen, and collagen is what gives skin its firmness. That established role is the basis for the appearance claims. No published trial has tested mega-dose orange juice for skin, so whether intake beyond adequacy changes how skin looks has not been studied. Wikipedia describes the health value of orange juice as debatable because of its high sugar content.
quick.how: People drink orange juice daily or take vitamin C, often alongside other citrus and fruit. Skin changes are reported over weeks.
quick.risks: Doses above about 3,000 mg/day have caused diarrhea and other gastrointestinal effects, and the US upper level is 2,000 mg/day. Orange juice is high in sugar.

angle.text: Users drink orange juice or take large amounts of vitamin C to support collagen and brighten skin. Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis, which is the route to firmer-looking skin. Whether high intake changes appearance has not been tested.

cinnamon-apple-cider-vinegar-shots.summary: Diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes with cinnamon, taken for less bloating, fat loss and clearer skin.

quick.overview:
ACV shots are small servings of diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes mixed with cinnamon, drunk to reduce bloating, help fat loss and clear skin. Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice to alcohol and then to acetic acid, and is about 5% acetic acid.

The chain: proponents attribute effects to acetic acid, which they say curbs appetite and moderates blood sugar, leading to a leaner midsection. Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use affects body weight, blood sugar or lipids, and that health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.
quick.how: People mix a small amount of vinegar into water, sometimes adding cinnamon, and drink it daily, often before meals. Users report judging effects over several weeks.
quick.risks: Diluted moderate use is generally described as low-risk. Reported harms include tooth-enamel erosion, throat and esophageal irritation, digestive upset, and burns when applied to skin or eyes. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted.

angle.text: Home-made apple cider vinegar shots, sometimes with cinnamon, are taken to reduce bloating, curb appetite and clear skin, with a leaner midsection as the goal. The effect is attributed to acetic acid. Reviews report no high-quality trials of regular use for weight.

fat-burner-supplements.summary: Stimulant-based supplement blends sold to raise calorie burn and curb appetite for a leaner, more defined look.

quick.overview:
Fat burners are over-the-counter supplement blends, often built around caffeine-type stimulants and plant extracts, sold to raise metabolism or cut body fat. Users take them to speed fat loss and get a leaner, more defined look.

The chain: the marketed effect is higher energy expenditure and lower appetite, often called thermogenic, which adds up to a bigger calorie deficit. Mechanisms differ by ingredient and are not established for the blends as sold. The sources reviewed contain no efficacy data for the category as a whole, and individual ingredients vary widely in how much research exists.
quick.how: People take capsules or powders, usually in the morning or before training, alongside a calorie-controlled diet and exercise. Blends vary widely between products, so routines and ingredients differ.
quick.risks: Wikipedia's supplement overview reports that weight-loss products are a leading cause of supplement liver injury, that multi-ingredient products have been linked to more adverse events, and that many products with undeclared drugs were sold for weight loss. Stimulants can bring jitters and psychiatric effects. In the US they are sold without pre-market approval.

angle.text: Users take multi-ingredient stimulant blends to speed fat loss and get a leaner, more defined look. The blends aim to raise energy use and lower appetite, widening the calorie deficit. Blends vary widely between products, and efficacy has not been established at the category level.

green-tea-egcg.summary: Green tea and its catechin EGCG, taken as tea or extract as a mild fat-burner to help get leaner.

quick.overview:
Green tea and its main catechin, EGCG, are taken as a gentle thermogenic for fat loss, either as tea or as concentrated capsule extracts. People use it to help get leaner over time.

The chain: catechins are said to mildly raise thermogenesis and fat oxidation, shifting body composition slightly. Dried green tea leaves contain about 7,380 mg of EGCG per 100 g, far more than black tea. Most published work is laboratory or animal research, for example in diet-induced obese mice, and reviews describe poor oral absorption. The sources reviewed contain no completed human trial showing an appearance effect.
quick.how: People drink green tea through the day or take a green tea extract capsule, often alongside a calorie-controlled diet and training. Any effect is expected to be mild and to build over months.
quick.risks: EFSA stated in 2018 that 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could increase liver-damage risk, and green tea catechins are among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury. The FDA has sent warning letters to EGCG makers over disease claims.

angle.text: Green tea and EGCG extracts are used as a mild fat-burner: catechins are said to slightly raise thermogenesis and fat oxidation, helping you get leaner over time. Support comes mostly from lab and animal studies, with human appearance outcomes less established.
